source_title: Science Francis Halzen Wins 2026 Nobel Prize In Physics For IceCube Neutrino Discovery
source_excerpt:
Belgian-American physicist Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for pioneering work that transformed the study of elusive subatomic particles known as neutrinos. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences recognised his decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos originating from astrophysical sources. Often described as ‘ghost particles’, neutrinos can pass through matter almost undisturbed.
Halzen’s work showed how the Antarctic ice could be turned into a giant detector, opening a new way of observing some of the universe’s most powerful and distant events.
Halzen realised that the vast quantities of clear ice beneath the South Pole could be used to detect neutrinos. These particles interact with matter extremely rarely, allowing them to travel through the Earth and human bodies almost unnoticed.
The idea led to the creation of IceCube, an enormous observatory buried deep beneath the Antarctic surface. The facility detects flashes of light produced when neutrinos collide with particles in the ice.
The observations have given scientists new information about where high-energy neutrinos come from and how they are produced. Researchers say the particles act as messengers from the cosmos, carrying information from distant galaxies and violent events such as exploding stars.

The Nobel committee praised Halzen’s leadership of an international team of scientists and engineers, saying his scientific vision and persistence had helped establish a new form of astronomy.
Halzen was previously recognised for his work on neutrinos, with Smithsonian magazine dubbing him ‘Neutrino Man’ in 2014. His IceCube project has since become a major tool for studying some of the universe’s most energetic phenomena.
The 2026 physics prize carries a monetary award of 12 million Swedish crowns, equivalent to about $1.2 million. The Nobel medals will be presented by Sweden’s King Carl XVI Gustaf at a ceremony in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death.
The physics award is the second Nobel announced this year, following the medicine prize. The chemistry prize is due to be announced on Wednesday.
